items.prompt: The document claims two primitive packages, a list of declared parameters, and that every other predicate is defined from them (Part XIV, Derivation 6). Hunt for anything still smuggled: a predicate used before or without definition, a definition that quietly uses 'represents', 'explains', 'is a cause', 'relevant', 'begs the question' or a judgement word, and any place where the instantiation relation Inst or the admitted edit set A_Theta is asked to do more than the document says the physical module supplies. Check the dependence order clause by clause; find any cycle, especially through (R), Con, Build, Deploy and Attempt.

Check every derivation and remark in Part XVI against the definitions it cites. For each: are the hypotheses stated sufficient; is the proof valid as written; does the stated consequence follow; is anything cited elsewhere in the document as stronger than what was proved? Pay particular attention to Derivation 1's injectivity hypothesis, Derivation 2's definition of account-equivalence, Derivation 3's closure hypothesis and 'admissible class', Derivation 5's question-organization (are its solutions exactly the coherently posed questions?), Derivation 6's claim that the Rep/Con cycle is broken, and Derivation 8's restriction on bijections.

Attack point (A) now targets the anchored grade of Account (Part V: properness, resolution, no global relation, world-kind on the admitted contract, actuality of route). Construct, as concretely as you can, a candidate that satisfies all six conjuncts of (E) and all four anchored conditions on an admitted contract with a non-declared transport, and that plainly explains nothing. If you cannot, say precisely which condition blocks each attempt (the one-component repackaging, a two-component split of it, a lookup with a proper decomposition, a decoy with the same world-kind). Also test whether the four anchored conditions exclude any genuine mechanism.

The revision makes contract adequacy ('C is not protective') a conjunct of Account itself, defined in Part V as: no admitted pair outside C at which the target's answer moves while the candidate's does not, or the reverse. Attack this. Is it well-defined (which baseline value; what if the candidate's translation is undefined at the pair)? Is it too strong (does it make every account on a restricted contract fail whenever the target has any out-of-scope dependence)? Too weak (can a scope exclude exactly the separating change and still pass)? Does it collide with the counterfactual set K, with Derivation 7's frozen assessment, or with the two-index treatment of objectivity in Grievance 4?

Part II now has forward kinds (signatures on the contract minus the baseline pairs, indexed to grain and contract) and historical kinds (predicates on the producing history), and Grievance 12 defends individuating transports by history but components by signature. Attack: does excluding the baseline pairs from 'separating changes' lose real distinctions (constants, initial conditions, things that differ only in state)? Is a historical kind well-defined without the provenance witnesses being available for components? Does the transport/component asymmetry hold up, or does the actuality-of-route condition in the anchored grade smuggle history into fidelity after all? Is the analysis-of-kinds conjecture (Part XV) now stated so that it could be refuted?

Part IV's selection witness now requires a population of at least two, an applied variation operator, a non-empty history with a non-trivial pair, a survival condition that eliminated at least one member, causal responsibility, non-triviality over the events, and blindness defined as absence of an itemised defect representation with scalar summaries allowed. Attack: is it still trivially satisfiable by some construction? Does 'causally responsible' reintroduce a primitive? Does the precedence rule (constructed over selected over declared) create cases where a plainly selected transport counts as constructed because some witness can be gerrymandered? Can every construction witness now be rewritten as a selection witness satisfying these clauses, or vice versa? Is the blindness definition consistent with Part X's construction witness?

Part III attaches provenance to the whole question, Part X adds a merit condition for found questions, Derivation 5 builds the question-organization, and Part X and XV state that inventing a new dimension of variation is not representable. Attack: is the merit condition either trivial (every constructed question repairs some obligation) or too strong? Does the question-organization's edit set admit exactly the changes needed, and is 'add a pair to K with a meaning' an edit an organization can have? Is the stated limit on concept creation actually a limit, or does some reading of Inst plus a new grain already cover it? Which of the four open cases in Part XV (impossibility, symmetry, artefact, mathematics) could be closed with what the document already has, and which cannot?

Find internal contradictions or tensions between parts of the revised document. Candidates: the orientation of transports in Part IV versus its use in (R), Account and Derivation 8; the two-place Account versus its uses in (K1), (EK) and Part VI; the six conjuncts of (E) versus any sentence still counting them; grain admissibility versus the declared-index status of grain; the exclusion of baseline pairs from kind identity versus Derivation 1's signature preservation on all of C; Part IV's claim that surprise on C entails loss of Deploy versus Part X; the historical index in Part VIII versus Derivation 7; the scenario in Derivation 10 versus the class membership claims of Part XIV; and anything else you find.

Document 20 is a revision of document 10; document 20a claims which defects were repaired and where. Audit 20a against the two texts: for each row marked Done, is the repair actually present in 20 and does it do what the row says? Find any defect of 10 that survives in 20 under new wording. Find any new defect that 20 introduces which 10 did not have. Rank by severity. Do not summarise; quote.
